# Notes Before the Crisis Call

*Written now, in the first hours, deliberately — because the document that matters is the one drafted before the sentiment data arrives and before anyone has calculated whose year this ruins. Anything assembled after those two things is not a strategy. It's a negotiated position.*

---

## The brief contains the first mistake

We've been asked to manage a crisis "caused by a cultural misunderstanding."

I'd let that phrase live in internal documents for exactly as long as it takes us to notice what it's doing, and I'd make sure it never reaches a microphone. *Misunderstanding* describes a symmetrical event — two parties, both partially wrong, no one at fault. What happened is that we said something and a large number of people understood it perfectly. They were not confused. They were insulted, and the fact that we didn't intend it is a statement about us, not about them.

Anyone who publicly frames this as a misunderstanding is arguing that the audience made an error. In a market where dignity is a live public value — and it usually is, in exactly the markets where this happens — that argument does more damage than the original ad, because the ad was careless and the defence is condescending. Carelessness is forgivable. Being told you misread the joke is not.

So: internal vocabulary, *harm we caused*. External vocabulary, the same. This is not humility as a tactic. It's that the alternative loses.

---

## An assumption I'd rather state than have someone discover in week three

I'll reason as though this is a market with the following shape, partly because it's where I've been working and partly because being specific in a wrong direction is more useful than being careful in a vague one: a high-context communication culture, a religiously or nationally significant symbol involved, a young and mobile-native population, a small number of dominant social platforms with extremely fast informal amplification, a regulator or ministry with genuine licensing leverage over broadcast and possibly over us, a domestic competitor who benefits, a distribution base of many thousands of small independent retailers who are absorbing this in person, and an existing cultural infrastructure for organised boycott.

If we're actually in a low-context, litigation-heavy, media-fragmented market with no regulatory exposure, roughly a third of what follows changes — mostly the sequencing and the role of the state. The structure holds. If someone in the room knows which case we're in, now is when saying so is nearly free.

---

## The three clocks, which are not the same clock

Most crisis failures I've watched were failures of tempo, not of judgement. Someone runs the whole response at the speed of the fastest clock and produces a legal position in twelve hours and a cultural repair in never.

**Clock one: hours.** Stop the bleeding. Everything here is subtractive and almost none of it requires approval.

**Clock two: days to three weeks.** Say the thing, be seen, absorb. This is where sincerity is either demonstrated or permanently forfeited.

**Clock three: two quarters and beyond.** Replace the association. Not repair — replace. This clock is the only one that determines whether we still have a business here in three years, and it's the one that gets no budget because by then the crisis is "handled."

Different owners for each. If the same person owns all three, clock three loses, every time, because clocks one and two generate visible relief and clock three generates invoices.

---

## Clock one — the first day, mostly things we stop doing

**Pull, don't pause.** Every placement, every platform, every version, including the ones in adjacent markets that nobody has found yet — and someone will find them, and the discovery of a still-live asset resets the entire clock to zero. "Paused pending review" is heard as *we're waiting to see if this blows over*, which is, to be fair, usually what it means.

**Stop all unrelated commercial posting in that market.** Cheerful product content running alongside a live grievance is its own second incident, and it's free to avoid. Somebody with a scheduling tool and no context will otherwise post something about a new flavour at 9am tomorrow.

**Don't explain the joke.** Not once, not in a background briefing, not in an internal note that will leak. The explanation is always some version of *what we actually meant was*, and it always reads as *you're not sophisticated enough to have got it*.

**Don't deploy the legal register.** No "we regret that some may have found." No conditional clauses. If our counsel needs a defensible non-admission for a regulatory filing, that document exists on a different track, in a different file, and it is never the public text. The two audiences cannot be served by one sentence, and the attempt to serve both produces the sentence everyone screenshots.

**Get the trade told before the public.** Our distributors and the independent retailers holding our stock are being asked about this across a counter, today, by people they've known for years. If they have nothing to say, they will either invent something or quietly stop facing our product forward — and the second one is the expensive one, because shelf presence lost in a fortnight takes two years to rebuild. A one-clause line, in the local language, that a shopkeeper can repeat without embarrassment, is worth more than the press release. Same for our own staff in-market, who are absorbing this at family dinners.

**Separate the fabrications from the grievance.** Within a day there will be doctored versions, invented quotes, and a claim we did something worse than we did. Correct facts, flatly, once, without heat. Never correct feelings. The distinction matters: arguing about what we actually published is legitimate; arguing about whether people should be upset is suicide.

---

## Clock two — who speaks, and in what grammar

**Not headquarters.** A global CMO apologising in English from another continent communicates that the injured market is a line item being managed. The speaker should be the most senior person who actually lives there, by name, on camera, in the local language, unscripted enough to be believed, once — and then available rather than broadcasting.

I'd note in passing that this is the moment when our own attitude to hierarchy gets tested in public. The instinct will be to route the response upward, because the stakes feel large. The stakes being large is precisely the argument for the opposite: legitimacy here comes from proximity, not rank, and an apology delivered from a level of the organisation that has never been in the market is not an apology, it's an announcement.

**The grammar of the apology, which is not a style question.** In most of the markets where this happens, an apology has required components and their absence is legible instantly:

- Name the harm, specifically. Not "content some found offensive" — the actual thing, the actual symbol, the actual community.
- Apologise *to* named parties, not to the air.
- No conditionals. "If anyone was offended" contains an accusation.
- Accept responsibility without distributing it. Blaming the agency is technically often accurate and is heard as *we are still looking for someone else to be at fault*. The agency relationship is a separate matter, handled later, and not as a public sacrifice.
- Say what changes. Vague future care is worthless; a specific structural change is the only part anyone remembers.
- Then stop talking. A second apology is worse than a first one, because it reveals the first was a trial balloon.

**Ask before deciding what would help.** The instinct is to announce a remedy — a donation, a programme, a partnership — inside the apology, because it converts a passive statement into an active one. I'd resist that for about seventy-two hours and go to credible local figures first, including ones who have criticised us, with a genuinely open question: what would make this right, and what would make it worse? Two outcomes, both useful. We find remedies we wouldn't have thought of, and we find out which remedies would have been read as buying our way out. A donation to a recipient *we* selected is a purchase. A remedy shaped by the people harmed is a concession. They cost the same and they land completely differently.

I'd also expect the useful version of this feedback to arrive indirectly — as a suggestion about what a hypothetical brand might do, or a story about someone else's mistake. If we send someone to those conversations who only recognises information when it arrives as a direct recommendation, we'll come back with nothing and report that everyone was very understanding.

**Costly signals, because words are free and everyone knows it.** Apologies are cheap and the audience prices them accordingly. What moves belief is something we obviously didn't want to do:

- Standing creative authority given to a named local body — with actual kill rights, published, not advisory. A veto that can only be exercised by people whose careers depend on the campaign shipping is not a veto.
- A consequence visible in our own structure. I'd stop short of firing a junior person as theatre — that's understood everywhere as a sacrifice, and it signals that we protect the people who set the incentives. If accountability lands, it lands where the approval authority was.
- Money, but structural and long — a multi-year commitment to something the market chose, rather than a cheque with a photograph.

The test for any of these: would a cynical nineteen-year-old in that market describe it as *they actually gave something up*, or as *they hired a PR firm*? If the second, don't announce it; just do it quietly and let it be discovered.

---

## Clock three — replacing the association, not repairing it

Here's the part I'd argue hardest for, and probably sideways, because it's the part that gets cut.

We're not going to restore the previous narrative. That version of the brand in that market is gone; a search on our name now returns this, and will for a while. The realistic objective isn't erasure, it's displacement — accumulating enough newer, more useful associations that the incident becomes a thing that happened rather than the thing we are.

Two working principles:

**Reappear with product, not with contrition.** The most common overcorrection is a follow-up campaign of reverent homage to the culture we offended — heritage imagery, respectful voiceover, local craftspeople. This is the fastest available route to a second incident, because it is transparently penitential and because reverence performed by an outsider is its own category of insult. Better: go quiet on brand advertising for a season, keep the product excellent and available, be visibly present in ordinary commercial life, and return to a normal register — including, eventually, humour — later than feels comfortable.

**Earn back through utility, in the trade.** Reputation with the public is repaired in public. Reputation with the thousands of small retailers who decide whether we're on the shelf is repaired by showing up, absorbing their losses rather than passing them down, and not pulling investment from the market in the quarter where the numbers look bad. That last one is the real test and it will be made in a finance review, not a communications meeting, by someone protecting a global margin line. Whoever cuts in-market trade support in month two to fund the crisis response will have solved the crisis and lost the distribution, and the two facts will be reported by different people.

---

## The cause, which is almost certainly not creative judgement

I'd want somebody outside the reporting line of everyone involved to establish one fact within a week: **did anyone flag it?**

The pattern is boringly consistent. A concept developed centrally, adapted by translation rather than re-conceived, approved on a timeline set by a media buy, with a local objection that either wasn't raised, or was raised and overruled, or — the case I'd bet on — was raised in the local idiom, indirectly and politely, as a question about whether the timing was ideal, and was recorded by someone from a direct-communication culture as *local team had minor comments, no blockers*.

If that's what happened, then the failure is our listening architecture, not our creative process, and every fix aimed at approval checklists will produce the same incident again with a different symbol in about four years. The correct fix is uncomfortable and structural: local authority to stop, exercisable without escalation, held by someone who doesn't need to justify it in the vocabulary of the centre. Which is a genuine transfer of power and will therefore be resisted, and the resistance will be framed as concern about brand consistency.

And whatever we find — publish the corrective inside the company before we announce it outside. If the market hears about our new local veto before our own regional teams do, they'll correctly read it as a message to the press.

---

## Tests fixed now, before the evidence arrives

Because criteria written afterwards are commentary, and because the sentiment dashboard will start producing comforting numbers by day nine.

**Volume of mentions is not the metric.** It always declines. It declines whether we handled this well or not, because attention is finite. Measuring recovery by mention volume is measuring the news cycle and calling it forgiveness.

**The real gates:**

- Do our independent-trade retailers still face our product forward at twelve weeks? Shelf presence is the only honest read on whether the people who deal with our customers in person think we're still defensible.
- Repeat purchase in the affected market at twelve weeks against pre-incident baseline. Trial will recover first and mean nothing.
- Does the incident still attach to our name in the search behaviour of an ordinary shopper at six months, or only in the search behaviour of journalists?
- Are we able to recruit in that market? Employees are the most sensitive instrument we have and the last one anyone checks.
- Can a nineteen-year-old who doesn't work for us defend us in one clause, in the local language, without our help? That's the same test I'd apply to a product concept, and it's the same reason: if our position can't be carried by someone with no incentive to carry it, we don't have a position, we have a press office.
- At six months, is the local veto still real — has it actually stopped something, and did anyone senior lose that argument? An unexercised safeguard is decoration.

---

## The failure modes, in order of likelihood

**One.** The response gets written to protect the person who approved the campaign. It will be subtle — a slightly softer verb, a clause about industry-wide challenges, an internal review that concludes the process was sound but the execution was unfortunate. This is the most probable outcome and the hardest to name, because everyone involved will be behaving reasonably.

**Two.** The crisis becomes a document. A learnings deck, a revised toolkit, a mandatory module, and no change to who can stop what. Six months later the toolkit exists as a fact inside the organisation and the case for having responded well has quietly become the case for not having wasted the quarter.

**Three.** We recover, decide the market is structurally hostile, and reduce investment — converting a repairable incident into a permanent retreat, with a rationale assembled afterwards that will sound like strategy.

The defence against all three isn't discipline or good intentions. It's that clock three has a named owner, a protected budget, and a reporting line that doesn't pass through anyone whose bonus this incident threatens.

---

One thing I'd do on purpose: put the strongest local critical voice we can get into a room with the global brand team, in the first fortnight, before positions harden and while everyone is still frightened enough to listen. Not a briefing — an actual argument, watched rather than managed. If that conversation is comfortable, we've learned nothing about who will hold the line when a campaign with a media commitment behind it comes up against a local objection next spring.

We aren't repairing a message. We're re-establishing whether we're the kind of organisation that can hear something before it's shouted — which is the same capability that would have prevented this, and the only one worth buying with a crisis.
